title: Hubbis Macro Corner: Fed Tightening, EM Conviction and AI’s Broader Capital Cycle Reshape Portfolio Positioning - Hubbis
text:
Exit Full Page News Investments Hubbis Macro Corner: Fed Tightening, EM Conviction and AI’s Broader Capital Cycle Reshape Portfolio Positioning Investments Hubbis Macro Corner: Fed Tightening, EM Conviction and AI’s Broader Capital Cycle Reshape Portfolio Positioning Sep 21, 2026 Hubbis At a Glance The Federal Reserve has returned to tightening, but the investment debate has shifted towards how far it ultimately needs to go. The Fed raised rates by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00% on 16 September, with updated projections pointing to the possibility of at least one further increase this year. UBS sees the subsequent repricing as creating better opportunities in quality fixed income, while J.P. Morgan Asset Management expects inflation and growth to cool into 2027, potentially limiting the eventual tightening cycle. Source: UBS | J.P. Morgan Asset Management . Emerging markets are moving back up institutional allocation agendas. BlackRock Investment Institute moved back to an overweight in emerging-market equities, citing stronger earnings growth, more attractive valuations than the US and reduced leverage concerns. State Street Investment Management also finds emerging-market debt relatively resilient despite rising US yields, particularly at shorter durations. Source: BlackRock | State Street . AI remains a powerful earnings and investment theme, but the opportunity set is broadening. Lombard Odier sees AI, defence spending, energy security and trade-driven industrial investment combining into a wider global manufacturing revival, while State Street warns that technological success does not guarantee investment success for today’s dominant companies. Source: Lombard Odier | State Street . Higher yields are improving income opportunities while making duration selection more important. Goldman Sachs attributes the global yield reset to a combination of fiscal borrowing, AI financing, resilient growth and energy pressures, while Nuveen sees floating-rate senior loans as particularly useful in a volatile rates environment. Source: Goldman Sachs | Nuveen . The global tightening cycle is becoming increasingly differentiated. The European Central Bank raised rates earlier in the period, the Bank of England held at 3.75% while warning of higher inflation risks, and the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to 1.25% this morning. The Japanese decision arrived too close to this report’s cut-off for meaningful institutional post-decision research to have been published, so it is treated as a late-breaking development rather than a research view. Investment research published this week suggests that markets are moving into a more complicated phase of the 2026 cycle. Corporate earnings remain supportive, artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending continues to expand and global economic growth has proved more resilient than many investors expected. Yet the Federal Reserve has now returned to tightening, long-term government yields are around multi-year or multi-decade highs in several markets, oil remains above USD100 a barrel and governments are competing with the private sector for an increasingly expensive pool of capital. The result is less a wholesale move away from risk than a reassessment of where risk is being taken and how investors are being compensated for it . Emerging markets, floating-rate credit, industrials, infrastructure and selected areas beyond megacapitalisation technology are gaining attention, while long-duration assets and highly concentrated thematic exposures increasingly require explicit conviction. The Fed Hikes — but the Bigger Question Is What Comes Next Ahead of the Federal Open Market Committee meeting, J.P. Morgan Asset Management argued that the Fed had effectively placed itself in a position where failing to raise rates would risk undermining its own credibility. Chair Kevin Warsh had repeatedly emphasised the importance of returning inflation towards target, while oil prices, resilient employment and a slightly firmer August inflation reading had pushed market expectations overwhelmingly towards a September increase. By 14 September, the futures market was pricing a 92% probability of a hike. Source: J.P. Morgan Asset Management . The Fed duly raised its target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00% on 16 September . UBS described the decision as hawkish: the two-year Treasury yield rose to 4.72%, the 10-year held close to 5%, and the Fed’s updated projections showed a median policy-rate estimate of 4.1% for 2026, consistent with another increase before year-end. Markets subsequently moved towards pricing three additional hikes by mid-2027. Source: UBS . The longer-term implications remain less clear. J.P. Morgan expects both growth and inflation to cool as 2027 approaches and argued before the meeting that, even after a September increase, the Fed might ultimately require only one additional hike — or potentially none — in December. Its portfolio conclusion remained constructive towards core fixed income for yield, international equities for total return and alternatives for differentiated sources of alpha and income. Source: J.P. Morgan Asset Management . That stands in contrast to some of the more hawkish pre-meeting research. State Street Investment Management argued on 15 September that core inflation remained insufficiently subdued and that the balance of inflation risks justified further tightening. The divergence reinforces a theme seen repeatedly this year: the most useful portfolio decision may not be predicting the exact number of Fed moves, but ensuring portfolios can tolerate several plausible outcomes. Source: State Street . The Bond Sell-Off Is Bigger Than the Fed Goldman Sachs Research argued on 15 September that the increase in global government yields is being driven by more than expectations for central-bank policy. Fiscal deficits, defence spending, AI-related corporate borrowing, resilient economic growth and higher energy prices are all competing for the same global pool of savings. The fact that yields have risen while bond-market volatility has remained relatively contained suggests that the repricing is fundamentally driven rather than simply a technical dislocation. Source: Goldman Sachs . That competition for capital has important consequences for long-duration assets. Governments need to finance large fiscal programmes at the same time as hyperscalers and infrastructure developers raise capital for data centres, chips, power networks and other elements of the AI build-out. Higher yields therefore reflect not only inflation expectations but also the increasing price required to allocate scarce capital between competing borrowers. Nuveen reached a similar conclusion from a fixed-income perspective. Its 14 September weekly commentary showed the US 10-year Treasury at 4.97% and the 30-year at 5.35% after oil prices above USD100 a barrel reignited inflation fears and a Treasury buyback disappointed market expectations. Nuveen nevertheless regarded the move as an overshoot rather than necessarily the start of an uncontrolled bond sell-off, arguing that higher yields were creating better opportunities in high-quality duration, particularly municipal bonds. Source: Nuveen fixed-income commentary . State Street’s 17 September fixed-income research took the debate a step further. It argued that bonds can still provide portfolio stability despite persistent inflation, less dependable stock-bond correlations and volatile government yields, but that investors may need a broader toolkit rather than relying disproportionately on conventional sovereign duration. Income, credit selection and diversification across fixed-income sectors become more important in that environment. Source: State Street. Floating-Rate Credit Gains Appeal Nuveen’s CIO commentary identified senior loans and collateralised loan obligations (CLOs) as particularly relevant where policy rates may remain higher and Treasury yields volatile. Because senior-loan coupons reset with short-term rates, they carry materially less duration sensitivity than conventional fixed-rate bonds. As of 10 September, Nuveen calculated a yield to three-year of 9.02% for senior loans. Source: Nuveen . The Morningstar LSTA US Leveraged Loan Index had returned 3.28% year-to-date through 10 September, versus a 1.31% decline for the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index. Credit fundamentals have also improved: default activity has fallen to roughly 2% from around 4.5% in 2020, while stronger issuers generally retain manageable leverage and healthier interest coverage. That does not make the asset class indiscriminately attractive. Nuveen sees increasingly wide dispersion between stronger companies and borrowers facing refinancing, business-model or leverage pressure. New issuance is also returning as companies refinance maturities and finance leveraged acquisitions, potentially creating opportunities where investors are compensated with better spreads, structures or documentation. Source: Nuveen . For private wealth, the broader point is that fixed income no longer needs to be expressed predominantly through long-duration government or investment-grade bonds. Floating-rate credit can offer a different combination of income, duration and credit exposure, although the trade-off is greater issuer and liquidity risk. Emerging Markets Move Back into Focus BlackRock Investment Institute moved back to an overweight view on emerging-market equities in its 14 September weekly commentary. Earnings durability was central to the change. BlackRock sees emerging-market earnings growth accelerating while valuations remain materially below the US, and believes the leverage concerns that prompted it to move neutral in June — particularly in Korea — have eased following deleveraging. Source: BlackRock weekly commentary . This is noteworthy because higher US interest rates have historically been treated as an automatic headwind for emerging markets. BlackRock’s argument is more nuanced: if yields are increasing because investment and growth are strong, earnings can offset part of the valuation pressure. Emerging-market equities currently combine faster earnings growth with substantially lower valuation multiples than US equities, giving them a different starting point as the global cost of capital resets. State Street’s emerging-market debt review, published on 15 September, similarly found the asset class relatively resilient during August’s rate repricing. Shorter-duration hard-currency bonds had outperformed longer maturities, while sovereign spreads remained comparatively stable even as higher US term premia and fiscal concerns pushed Treasury yields upwards. The implication is not that emerging-market debt has become immune to developed-market rates, but that duration and country selection can matter more than the broad asset-class label. Source: State Street emerging-market debt commentary . BlackRock’s broader September framework remains constructive on both US and emerging-market equities while favouring short- and medium-term government bonds over long maturities. Its reasoning links the two views: stronger earnings can support equities in a higher-rate environment, while long sovereign bonds carry greater exposure to fiscal issuance, inflation and term-premium risk. AI Moves Beyond Technology and into the Industrial Economy Lombard Odier’s 15 September research identified AI, defence, trade policy and energy security as four forces behind a broader revival in global manufacturing. AI remains the leading driver, but the investment cycle increasingly encompasses physical infrastructure, industrial equipment, electricity generation, defence manufacturing and supply-chain reconfiguration. Source: Lombard Odier . That broadening is important for equity portfolios because it creates earnings beneficiaries beyond the companies designing chips or operating cloud platforms. Rising capital expenditure in energy, infrastructure, defence and advanced manufacturing can support industrials and other cyclical sectors while reducing — at least at the margin — the market’s dependence on a small group of US technology companies. Lombard Odier said this wider investment cycle underpins its global equity overweight. UBS reached a complementary conclusion in its weekly House View. Oracle’s latest cloud results reinforced the strength of demand for AI computing capacity, while growing debate around AI safety and the pace of frontier-model development introduced a new source of uncertainty. UBS does not expect calls for stronger safeguards to end the AI capital-expenditure cycle and continues to favour diversified exposure across the value chain rather than one narrow segment. Source: UBS weekly House View . The Dot-Com Comparison Is Becoming More Useful — but Not in the Obvious Way State Street’s 16 September research argued that investors may be drawing the wrong lesson from comparisons between AI and the dot-com bubble. The internet did transform the global economy, but many of the companies that financed or built the early infrastructure failed to remain dominant investments. A technology can succeed spectacularly without every early market leader capturing an adequate share of the eventual economic return. Source: State Street . This distinction is increasingly relevant as AI investment moves from building infrastructure towards adoption and monetisation. Investors need to distinguish between the durability of the technology itself and the durability of individual companies’ competitive advantages. High capital requirements, technological change and eventual commoditisation can redistribute value even while aggregate demand continues growing. The point also reinforces the case for broader equity exposure. If AI becomes embedded throughout the economy, part of its value may ultimately be captured by companies using the technology to improve productivity, pricing, margins and customer economics rather than solely by the businesses building the underlying models and infrastructure. Tactical Equity Signals Remain Positive, but Valuations Matter State Street’s 15 September tactical asset-allocation review remained moderately constructive on equities. Economic activity has stayed resilient, hiring has broadened and corporate fundamentals remain healthy, while new-business formation and labour-market indicators do not point towards an imminent deterioration in growth. Its models nevertheless identify valuations as a constraint, leaving the balance of signals consistent with positive but more moderate expected returns. Source: State Street tactical asset allocation . BlackRock similarly maintained its overweight in US equities while adding an overweight to emerging markets. The common rationale is earnings: higher rates are less threatening when they accompany stronger investment and economic activity and when profits are rising quickly enough to offset a higher discount rate. That does not eliminate valuation risk, but it changes the case from one of indiscriminate risk-taking to one of identifying where earnings growth remains durable. Source: BlackRock . Central-Bank Divergence Remains a Currency and Duration Risk Amundi Investment Institute’s 14 September weekly research highlighted how differently major central banks are now responding to the same energy shock. The European Central Bank increased its deposit rate to 2.50% and raised its inflation forecasts, while Amundi argued that the recent rise in energy prices had increased the probability that inflation would remain persistent. It continued to favour flexibility within fixed income rather than relying heavily on one duration position. Source: Amundi Investment Institute . The Bank of England took a different approach on 17 September, leaving Bank Rate unchanged at 3.75% by a six-to-three vote while acknowledging a larger upside inflation risk from energy. Three committee members preferred an immediate increase to 4%. The bank also paused active gilt sales, providing some relief to the long end of the UK curve. Japan then moved in the opposite direction this morning. The Bank of Japan raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 1.25% , its highest level in 31 years, in a seven-to-two vote. The yen initially weakened after the decision, suggesting that much of the move had already been priced and that markets are now more interested in the pace of subsequent normalisation. The announcement landed only shortly before this report’s cut-off, so no substantive post-meeting institutional research has yet been incorporated. For global private wealth, this divergence increases the importance of treating currency exposure separately from underlying asset selection. A Japanese equity allocation, a yen position and Japanese government bonds now represent increasingly different macroeconomic exposures, just as euro, sterling and US-dollar assets carry distinct monetary-policy paths. What This Might Mean for Wealth Managers and Family Offices Rate risk should be decomposed rather than treated as one bond-market decision. The Fed has tightened, but long-term yields are responding to fiscal borrowing, AI financing, energy and term premia as well as central-bank policy. Short-, medium- and long-duration bonds therefore offer very different risk profiles even when they share the same sovereign issuer. Income opportunities have improved, but the source of income matters. Quality government and corporate bonds now offer materially higher yields, while senior loans and CLOs can provide floating-rate income with less duration exposure. The trade-off is that credit selection, liquidity and refinancing risk become more important. Source: Nuveen . Emerging-market allocations warrant another look, but broad benchmarks can still conceal concentration. Strong AI-related earnings across parts of Asia, improving external fundamentals and attractive valuations support the case for selected EM assets. Higher US rates are still relevant, but this cycle demonstrates that the reason yields are rising can be as important as the direction of yields itself. Source: BlackRock . AI exposure should increasingly include both beneficiaries and adopters. The first phase of the investment cycle rewarded infrastructure providers. The next phase will test which companies across industrials, financials, healthcare, energy and other sectors can convert AI adoption into durable productivity and earnings improvements. Technological success does not guarantee that today’s largest beneficiaries retain the greatest share of future economic value. Portfolio diversification should be tested economically, not cosmetically. Owning technology equities, data-centre infrastructure, AI-linked credit and Asian semiconductor markets may look diversified by asset class and geography while remaining dependent on the same capital-expenditure cycle. Similarly, a portfolio spread across several long-dated developed-market bond markets can remain heavily exposed to the same inflation and term-premium shock. The broad message from this week’s research is therefore still constructive, but with greater emphasis on breadth, income and selectivity . The Fed’s return to tightening has not derailed corporate earnings or the AI investment cycle, while emerging markets and previously overlooked cyclical sectors are attracting greater institutional attention. At the same time, the higher cost of capital means that investors are being asked to distinguish more carefully between strong themes and strong investments, between income and duration, and between apparent diversification and genuine diversification. ** Disclaimer This article has been prepared by Hubbis for general information and editorial purposes only.
